Area.evidence_source: [page/8/Text/3] There were others, however, who admitted to emotional distress and who to some extent identified with those who had attempted suicide, confessing that they themselves did not have the courage to pursue this path. [page/8/Text/7] He was one of a group of four self-confessed 'no balls' participants with low self-esteem, who also said they had little control of their lives. [page/8/Text/7] Of the other three, one appeared to have had a serious mental illness, describing being diagnosed and treated for psychosis; a second probably had a learning difficulty; the third, Graham, said he didn't have 'the guts to do it'. He was engaged in increasingly frequent episodes of binge drinking, and described low levels of mastery, with no hope of abstinence and little hope of avoiding further prison sentences: [page/8/Text/15] In some ways, therefore, this small group had more in common with multiple attempters, with few hopes for the future and significant problems of addiction, possibly representing a fractured reflexivity. They portrayed restricted agency in relation to making choices; suicide was out of bounds to them personally, whereas the iterative habit of substance use was easily taken up. [page/9/Text/3] Some of this group of 'young hoods' did disclose emotional distress, and two reported significant suicidal thoughts in response to adverse events. [page/9/Text/6] Aran's easy talk about emotional issues and the casual mention of a psychiatrist are possibly typical of a younger generations' willingness to engage in emotional discourse.
